reasons.D: Runs of short, flat declaratives reporting each figure's fate, deadpan mock-dread and a plain first-person observer come closest to the passage's clipped rhythm and dry irony.
reasons.A: Steady first-person observer with some short doom sentences ('Not one of them is ever struck'), but the sentences are longer and more balanced, and it ends with an earnest sermon the passage avoids.
reasons.C: Has the right mock-grave humour (the inquest, the gods over Troy), but the sustained second-person 'you' and the more literary set-piece openings shift the stance away from the passage's plain 'I'.
reasons.B: The most essayistic and argumentative: long compound sentences, polished aphorisms ('The tragedy is in the altitude') and hedged disclaimers, far from the passage's terse, deadpan reportage.
